title: Evernote for Android
lede: Nielsen Norman Group’s 2015 example of Material Design as “flat 2.0”: a mostly flat app with subtle shadows on the bar and the action button.
summary: A mostly flat note app with card panes and a shadowed round add button, cited by NN/g in 2015.

source.label: Nielsen Norman Group, Kate Moran, “Flat Design: Its Origins, Its Problems, and Why Flat 2.0 Is Better for Users” (27 September 2015)

evidence.note: Relies on the NN/g article text. Its screenshot of the app is only 512 × 446 px, too small to record visual detail.

styles.note: Partial fit, documented only: NN/g names it as Material-style flat 2.0, with shadows on the bar and the action button and a card metaphor.

context: NN/g calls “Google’s Material design language” “one example of flat 2.0 with the right priorities”, and says that the Evernote app for Android “provides a few subtle shadows on the navigation bar and the floating + button (add new). It also makes use of the card metaphor to display content as flat, layerable panes in a 3D space.” [NN/g](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/flat-design/).
interpretation: The article is the clearest statement of how Material relates to [flat design](style:flat-design): the fills stay flat, and a few shadows return only where they tell the user what can be touched.
next: Find a larger, dated image of the 2015 Android app, for example in a Wayback copy of evernote.com, before marking this reference observed.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The app belongs to Evernote. The screenshot on the NN/g page belongs to NN/g.
